t: Throne Inheritance: A Family Tree Walked in Preorder
o:
## Understanding the problem

The Successor recursion is a disguised definition of preorder traversal: state the person, then descend into their children in birth order. death merely tags a person as invisible - the traversal order itself never changes, and a dead person's descendants stay in the line of succession. The whole design therefore reduces to: maintain a rooted tree keyed by names plus a dead set; getInheritanceOrder walks the tree in preorder and filters out the dead.

Tracing Example 1: children map king -> (andy, bob, catherine), andy -> (matthew), bob -> (alex, asha). Preorder yields king, andy, matthew, bob, alex, asha, catherine; after death(bob) the same walk skips bob but still visits alex and asha.

Constraints matter: up to 100000 births can form a single chain, so deep recursion risks blowing the call stack in Python-style runtimes - an explicit-stack iteration is the robust choice. With at most 10 order queries, O(family size) per query is easily affordable, while birth and death should stay O(1).
k: Successor(x, curOrder) is exactly preorder traversal (node first, then children in birth order) - recognizing the disguise collapses the problem.
Death is a filter, not a deletion: dead nodes must remain in the tree so their subtrees stay reachable.
A 100000-deep pedigree makes recursion risky in some languages; an explicit stack sidesteps runtime recursion limits.

a.i: Store children lists in a hash map (birth order preserved by appending) and a hash set for deaths. Each getInheritanceOrder runs a plain recursive DFS from the king, emitting alive names. birth and death are pure O(1) bookkeeping.
s: children: name -> ordered list of child names; dead: set of names.
birth(parent, child): append child to children[parent].
getInheritanceOrder: DFS from king; emit a name iff not dead; recurse over children in stored order.
a.t: birth/death O(1) average; getInheritanceOrder O(P) - every living-or-dead person is visited once.
a.sp: O(P) - the tree plus recursion depth up to O(P).

a.n: Approach 2: Iterative DFS with an Explicit Stack
a.i: The same walk, but the stack lives on the heap: pop a person, emit them if alive, and push their children reversed so the oldest pops first. Immune to recursion-depth limits, which matters for a 100000-long lineage chain.
s: Push the king onto a stack.
Pop x; if x is not dead, append it to the order.
Push x's children onto the stack in reverse birth order.
Repeat until the stack empties; return the order.
a.t: Same asymptotics as Approach 1: O(P) per query, O(1) average updates.
a.sp: O(P) - explicit heap-allocated stack instead of call frames.

w:
Present Approach 1 for clarity, then note the recursion-depth caveat and show the iterative variant - that progression demonstrates judgment about real limits.

**Pitfalls.** Physically removing dead nodes, which orphans their subtrees; losing sibling birth order by sorting names instead of appending; forgetting that the king himself can die yet his descendants still inherit.

**Follow-ups.** Support thousands of queries via a persistent iterator that resumes mid-traversal; successor-after-person queries; O(1)-space Morris-style threading of the tree.
